 Action thrillers from the 1970s and 1980s had a charm that's hard to replicate. Police detectives chased criminals through neon-lit streets, undercover agents took down dangerous organizations, and crime-fighting heroes relied on fast cars, fists, and whatever gadgets the writers could dream of. Shows like Miami Vice and The A-Team became pop-culture events, complete with charismatic leads, memorable theme songs, and enough action to keep viewers coming back week after week.

 However, television has changed dramatically since then. Modern action thrillers on Prime Video and Netflix tend to favor tighter editing, more convincing fight scenes, and stories that develop beyond a villain-of-the-week formula. Rewatching some old-school shows can feel weird because you immediately spot clumsy special effects, painfully repetitive plots, and problematic treatment of marginalized people.
 Even shows that helped shape the genre can feel dated in ways that nostalgia once made easy to overlook. These eight old-school action thrillers each have a different reason why they could be a tough watch in 2026.
 'Police Woman' (1974 – 1978)
 Angie Dickinson's Groundbreaking Cop Show Has a Problematic Side
 Police Woman NBC 
 What It's About: Angie Dickinson stars as Sergeant Suzanne "Pepper" Anderson, an undercover detective who takes on high-risk assignments to catch criminals. Working alongside her colleagues in the Los Angeles Police Department, she tackles everything from drug rings to prostitution networks. Police Woman ranked among the first hour-long dramas to put a woman in the lead, and Dickinson won a Golden Globe Award for the role.
 Why It's Unwatchable Now: Police Woman deserves credit for putting a capable female police officer at the center of an action-oriented crime drama . However, the show's treatment of Pepper often undermines that achievement. Undercover assignments often require her to take on roles that sexualize her, with revealing costumes taking priority over believable police work. The problem becomes hard to ignore when the episodes rely on the heroine's appearance to make otherwise ordinary investigations more enticing.

 'The Fall Guy' (1981 – 1986)
 Cinematic Stunts Can't Save Its Repetitive Crime Stories
 What It's About: In The Fall Guy , Lee Majors stars as Colt Seavers, a Hollywood stuntman who supplements his income by tracking down bail jumpers. His stunt skills come in handy during reckless pursuits, while his younger cousin, Howie Munson (Douglas Barr), and fellow stunt performer, Jody Banks (Heather Thomas), help him tackle cases.
 Why It's Unwatchable Now: The premise works as a love letter to Hollywood craft, and the stunt work remains the main attraction. However, the surrounding stories don't always give it much competition. Colt typically takes on a simple case, gets into trouble, and uses his professional skills to escape before the credits roll. The formula suits a breezy episodic adventure, yet it offers little suspense once the pattern becomes obvious. The humor also feels dated and uneven.

 'The Six Million Dollar Man' (1974 – 1978)
 Slow-Motion Sprints and a Sound Effect That Never Clocks Out
 Close ABC 
 ABC

 What It's About: After a devastating accident, astronaut Steve Austin (Lee Majors) receives experimental bionic implants that give him superhuman strength, speed, and vision. He subsequently works for a secret government agency, taking on missions involving espionage, sabotage, and technology. The premise helped turn Austin into a pop-culture icon, and its spin-off, titled The Bionic Woman , gave the franchise a second hero.

 Why It's Unwatchable Now: The irony is that the show's signature action technique is also its biggest obstacle. Whenever Austin uses his bionic abilities, the series slows the footage down and adds its familiar electronic sound effect to emphasize his power. It was a clever visual shorthand at the time, but watching Austin jog, leap, or punch in slow motion over and over can make the action feel absurd and sluggish now.

 'Knight Rider' (1982 – 1986)
 A Talking Car Is Not Enough to Keep Every Episode Running
 What It's About: In Knight Rider , David Hasselhoff stars as Michael Knight, a crime fighter who works for the Foundation of Law and Government. His greatest asset is KITT, an artificially intelligent, self-aware, and nearly indestructible custom-made 1982 Pontiac Firebird Trans Am. Voiced by William Daniels, KITT is more than just a car. He's Michael's partner, sounding board, and occasional source of comic relief.
 Why It's Unwatchable Now: With a car that thinks, drives, and fights, Michael mostly poses and flirts. KITT solves all the problems, analyzes situations, and performs extraordinary feats. The practical effects and stunt work look modest today, while the cases Michael investigates almost always involve another shady businessman or a criminal organization. Once the novelty of a talking car wears off, Knight Rider has little to offer.

 'The Professionals' (1977 – 1983)
 Two Hard-Nosed British Agents Bring Their Ugly Attitudes Along
 Amazon 
 What It's About: The Professionals , a British action thriller, follows Bodie (Lewis Collins) and Doyle (Martin Shaw), two elite agents working for CI5, a fictional government security organization. Under the direction of George Cowley (Gordon Jackson), the pair tackle terrorism, kidnappings, political conspiracies, and other serious threats. The show also delivers several exciting car chases and gunfights.
 Why It's Unwatchable Now: The Professionals definitely has a more serious action-thriller foundation than some of its contemporaries, but the show's tough-guy attitude has aged poorly. Casually misogynistic remarks appear throughout the series, and Season 1, Episode 13, “Klansmen,” includes racist language and a storyline involving a white supremacist organization. The latter tackles a real social problem, but the language and presentation can make a modern rewatch uncomfortable.

 'Charlie's Angels' (1976 – 1981)
 Three Capable Detectives Are Reduced to Glamorous Eye Candy
 Close ABC 
 Cast of 'Charlie’s Angels' (1976–1981) ABC 
 Cast of 'Charlie’s Angels' (1976–1981) ABC 
 What It's About: Charlie's Angels became a symbol of 1970s television . It follows three private investigators who work for the Townsend Detective Agency under the direction of the mysterious Charlie, whose instructions arrive over a speakerphone. The original team features Kate Jackson as Sabrina Duncan, Farrah Fawcett as Jill Munroe, and Jaclyn Smith as Kelly Garrett.
 Together, the Angels tackle cases involving fraud, murder, kidnappings, and other crimes. The pilot of Charlie's Angels became one of the highest-rated TV movies in history, and the show's female leads were a major part of its appeal.

 Why It's Unwatchable Now: The problem is the gap between what the Angels can do and how the show presents them. They're trained investigators who routinely solve dangerous cases, yet their undercover missions often require bikinis, miniskirts, evening gowns, and other outfits designed to draw attention to their bodies.
 Charlie's Angels became closely associated with the term “ jiggle TV ,” a label that captures how frequently its presentation prioritizes sex appeal over detective work. The Angels also report to a male boss who remains largely unseen, reinforcing the idea that their independence still operates under male authority. The show broke ground by putting women in the lead roles of an action series, yet its approach is difficult to overlook.

 'The A-Team' (1983 – 1987)
 Ten Thousand Bullets Fly and Nobody Gets a Scratch
 NBC 
 What It's About: The A-Team follows four former U.S. Army Special Forces soldiers who become fugitives after being wrongly convicted of a crime. Led by Hannibal Smith (George Peppard), the group takes on jobs helping people in trouble while staying ahead of the military police. The team also includes con artist Face (Dirk Benedict), mechanic B.A. Baracus (Mr. T), and an eccentric pilot named H.M. Murdock (Dwight Schultz).
 Why It's Unwatchable Now: The A-Team is a defining show of the 1980s , thanks to its memorable characters, quotable dialogue, and instantly recognizable theme music. However, the action is pure cartoon. Cars flip, buildings explode, thousands of bullets fly in every episode, and nobody ever dies. The show essentially turns shootouts into slapstick, making it difficult to feel any genuine danger.

 'Miami Vice' (1984 – 1989)
 All Pastel, All Synth, and Not Much Left When the Music Stops
 What It's About: Created by Anthony Yerkovich and shaped by executive producer Michael Mann, Miami Vice follows undercover narcotics detectives Sonny Crockett (Don Johnson) and Ricardo Tubbs (Philip Michael Thomas) as they investigate drug trafficking and organized crime in Miami. The series stands apart through its use of contemporary music, striking cinematography, expensive cars, and neon-lit locations.
 Why It's Unwatchable Now: Miami Vice's visual identity was so influential that it helped redefine what a crime drama could look like on television. Of all the shows on this list, though, the thriller might have the hardest time escaping its own legacy. The style was gorgeous and revolutionary, but the same aesthetic can feel overpowering when revisiting the series in 2026.
 Miami Vice is filled with music-video montages, dramatic lighting, fashionable outfits, and moody pauses. All the while, the actual storytelling takes a back seat. The plots can also feel conventional, with Crockett and Tubbs investigating another drug kingpin, infiltrating another criminal network, or confronting another corrupt figure. Of course, dismissing Miami Vice as a dated action series would be unfair. The problem is that modern viewers may have to work through a lot of '80s excess to appreciate it.
